posts.title: Creators: Put One Good-Fit Sample First
posts.description: Want more good-fit brand inquiries? Put one sample for the audience you want near the top of your creator profile. A sponsor should not have to play scroll detective to see what you make. Imagine a balcony gardener pitching a neighborhood nursery. Put a short tomato-trellis clip for apartment gardeners first. The nursery can quickly see who the creator helps and the kind of post they could make together. This is an illustrative example, not a reported partnership or result. 🌱 Make one sample easy to judge Pick one kind of brand you genuinely want to work with. Put one sample that fits that brand and audience where visitors can find it quickly, then add a plain sentence about who the post helps. Send a few thoughtful pitches to brands that match. Count replies that mention the sample, ask about fit, or request a rate. That is a more useful sign than likes alone. If the replies miss, adjust the audience or idea before you film more. posts.title: More Local Orders Start With One Creator and One Clear Offer
posts.description: Want more local orders? Try one creator, one offer, and one clear next step. A small bakery does not need a famous creator to test creator marketing. It can ask one neighborhood food creator—someone whose posts already cover local food—to show a Saturday pastry box and tell viewers exactly how to preorder it. Keep the brief simple: show what is in the box, name the order deadline, and point to one preorder link. Make the paid partnership clear. Use a unique link or code so the bakery can count the orders or enquiries that came from the post. That gives you a useful signal. Likes are applause; preorders fill the oven schedule. A creator with a smaller, better-matched audience may be a stronger test than a large account whose followers live nowhere near the bakery. Treat that as a hypothesis to check, not a promise: sales depend on the offer, timing, audience, and how easy it is to order. One practical test Choose one offer people can act on now, such as a weekend box or a workshop seat.

posts.title: Run One Clear Ad Test Before You Raise the Budget
posts.description: Paid advertising can help a useful offer reach people who do not already follow your business. But if you change the audience, offer, image and budget all at once, spending money may still leave you guessing. Start with one offer, one audience and a budget small enough to learn from. Give the test one clear question Imagine a neighborhood bakery filling a Saturday cake-decorating workshop. This is an illustrative example, not a real Postly customer. Instead of advertising every product to everyone nearby, the bakery chooses one workshop, one local audience that can attend and one next step: reserve a seat. The question is whether that offer brings in workshop bookings at a cost the business can afford. Keep the offer, image and wording steady while you test one change. If you change the audience and the creative together, a difference in clicks or bookings will not tell you which change mattered.
